book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate

chapters.relation: Buckingham stages a phenomenology of a wasted café afternoon over three cups, arguing against a passage from Levinas's Nine Talmudic Readings that condemns the café as a 'non-place' where relaxing without obligation lets us tolerate the world's horrors. Against Levinas, he claims the coffeehouse's public 'solitude alongside others' sustains a courteous solidarity and, like the Epicurean Garden, offers necessary respite that fuels creative responsibility rather than evading the demand of the Other. He self-consciously adopts Levinas's own phenomenological method—attending to 'what is it like?'—to defend idling as the condition for responding to suffering with grace rather than grim duty.

Davids tastes Classic Red Brand X, Starbucks Guatemala Antigua, and the $100/lb Panama Esmeralda, and asks whether one can prove any coffee universally 'better.' He concedes taste is relative—citing East Asian dislike of acidity and the European relish for fermented 'rio-y' and Robusta notes North Americans call rotten—but escapes relativism via Stanley Fish's notion of 'interpretive communities': a dominant global community of expert cuppers shares assumptions and vocabulary (acidity, mouthfeel, sweetness, clean flavor) that let them rank the three coffees consistently. Legitimate evaluation is thus grounded not in the coffee itself but in the shared code of a community of judgment.

Wear traces the espresso aesthetic from the idealized, egalitarian Italian caffè—which he reads as an 'aestheticized Marxist' image of identical shots for businessman and street sweeper—to its dilution under neoliberal consumer choice, epitomized by the endless-customization L.A. Story 'half-caf twist of lemon' scene. He invokes Kant's Critique of Judgement and the sublime to argue that flavor and taste-judgment are neglected aesthetic faculties, and enlists the Frankfurt School (Adorno, Benjamin, Marcuse) and Bourdieu's cultural capital to explain how the market absorbs the espresso's beauty. He concludes that a single humble shot, as a memorial to the vast exploited labor chain behind it, is a truer aesthetic object than a branded frappuccino.

Hartmann argues the specialty-coffee 'third wave' (Stumptown, Intelligentsia, Counter Culture) could not exist without Starbucks, which taught consumers to pay for a boldly-roasted, ethically-branded, self-gifting aesthetic under neoliberalism. Drawing on Heidegger's thrownness and Gadamer's hermeneutical phenomenology, he punctures Nicholas Cho's claim that the third wave 'lets the coffee speak for itself': just as we perceive a chair as for-sitting through pre-given cultural meaning, cupping rituals actively build a coffee 'hermeneutic' that reshapes the drinker's very perception (the trained palate 'tastes' plantain and graham cracker). He likens this to ventriloquism—the coffee only 'speaks' because someone feeds it its lines—and uses Žižek's account of cynical ideology to expose the gap between fair-trade branding and reality.

Parker interviews Stumptown's director of operations Matt Lounsbury, probing for a single underlying value that unifies the roaster's ethics and aesthetics. Lounsbury insists quality—'how good the coffee can be'—is the gravitational center that pulls ethical behavior (record-breaking direct-trade prices, building washing stations in Rwanda, full health care for baristas, the Meet the Producers program) into orbit, while Parker suspects a deeper commitment to community and justice. The exchange enacts the book's recurring ethics/aesthetics entanglement: whenever asked about one, Lounsbury 'slips into' the other, framing direct trade as a win-win-win business model rather than idealism.

Bramucci and Mulholland use Kenyan smallholder farmers—Lucy Wanja, David Gachigi, Henry Maina, who earn $0.02–$0.10 per pound for coffee sold north for $12—to argue that fair-trade certification, while an improvement, secures only a 'minimum' wage and leaves growers trapped by mills, middlemen, and depressed global prices. They advance direct trade (Intelligentsia, Stumptown, and the author's own Safi Coffee, which makes farmers shareholders and pays up to twenty-fold more) as a more genuinely just alternative that invests in producers' long-term capacity. The ethical claim is that 'fair' as a sticker falls short of real equity, and that consumers' smug conscience is only earned by paying beyond the fair-trade minimum.

Kirkwood argues that caffeine is uncontroversially a performance-enhancing drug—boosting memory, reaction time, endurance—and that by WADA's own three-part test (performance-enhancing, potentially harmful, against the spirit of sport) coffee should count as doping, yet never has. He dismantles the standard anti-doping arguments as applied to coffee: the cheating/unfairness charge is circular and dissolves when everyone may use it; the 'unnaturalness' argument commits a non sequitur (umbrellas are unnatural too, and chewed coffee beans seem natural); and the harm test fails because the positive threshold sits at a mere 20-ounce serving, far below caffeinism. His conclusion is that coffee escapes the 'doping' label not through moral reasoning but through public acceptance—the emotive word 'drug' is withheld from the substance everyone uses.

Aleman, an ethnobotanist, asks 'Is coffee green?' and unpacks the many senses of 'green' (raw bean, naïve, money, and ecologically friendly) before weighing coffee's growth, organic and shade-grown methods, fair trade, globalization, and value chain. She judges coffee greenest at the source (shade-grown farms preserve migrating-bird habitat) but least green in the fossil-fueled journey from Global South farm to Global North cup, invoking Vandana Shiva's claim that 'drinking coffee is a political act' and Rigoberta Menchú on coffee and indigenous survival. She concludes the answer is partly subjective—withholding final judgment while resolving to keep drinking fair-trade, organic, shade-grown, single-source coffee—and warns of the cognitive dissonance, mirroring oil dependence, between judging coffee ungreen and drinking it anyway.

Keleher applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics to coffee, arguing that eudaimonia (flourishing, not mere pleasant feeling) is rational activity in accordance with virtue, that the human ergon is reason, and that money, pleasure, and honor are only instrumental to it. She illustrates the golden mean and phronêsis with coffee choices—the temperate drinker like Katherine or Samantha calibrates cups to her own tolerance and circumstances rather than a fixed number—and distinguishes the truly virtuous drinker from the merely continent one who still craves the forbidden 750-calorie frappuccino. She coins the minor virtue of 'javavity,' the habit of drinking good coffee the right way for the right reasons with the right feeling, and suggests that were Aristotle alive, coffee would join his 'external goods,' the proper equipment for doing noble acts.

The Coffee Bean Guys (James Kirkland and Dan Levy) deliver a comic afterword sending up both Hollywood hustle and philosophy itself, joking that philosophy is 'the science of getting high and asking: Why?'—which is what they do all day at a West Hollywood Coffee Bean & Tea Leaf while accomplishing nothing. Their running gag insists coffee is a drug ('wake up and smell the coffee you spilled on yourself') and that appearances matter more than reality: look busy, do nothing, and people will give you money. It is satire rather than argument, but it plays on the book's themes of coffee as stimulant, coffeehouse as workplace, and the caffeinated thinker who thinks hard and does little.

holes.name: Interpretive Communities
holes.what: Stanley Fish's thesis that meaning and evaluation arise not from an object itself but from the shared assumptions and vocabulary of a community of readers/judges.
holes.why: Chapter 24's entire escape from taste relativism rests on Fish's interpretive communities of expert coffee cuppers, and the taxonomy has no philosopher for Fish nor a concept capturing this community-grounded theory of judgment.
